newsitem.title: USA: Florida using RICO against tobacco companies.
newsitem.headline: Florida using RICO against tobacco companies.

text.p: Florida's state government on Friday faces off against the U.S. tobacco industry, using anti-racketeering laws and claiming big cigarette companies conspired to muddle health worries among Americans.

The new claim was tacked onto Florida's existing lawsuit seeking $1 billion or more from cigarette manufacturers and may expand the tobacco industry's financial exposure, according to tobacco-litigation expert Christopher Mueller of the University of Colorado School of Law.
"Florida has a good law (for winning its damage claims against tobacco companies) but it only goes back to 1994. Using RICO may give the state a deeper reach," Mueller said.

RICO, for Florida's Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act, is similar to laws in other states. Texas and other states have also used RICO laws to bolster claims against Philip Morris Cos Inc and other big tobacco companies. Mueller said successful use of RICO could add to the tobacco industry's potential financial losses to victims of cancer-connected diseases by allowing Florida to make claims for deaths and health costs before 1994.

Florida Attorney General Bob Butterworth is scheduled to appear on Friday in Palm Beach County Court in West Palm Beach, a spokesman said. He and attorneys for tobacco companies will argue over the industry's request that the RICO claim be dismissed.
It was unclear when a ruling would be made, a court official said.

Presiding Palm Beach County Circuit Judge Harold Cohen recently dismissed 15 counts of the state government's 18-count lawsuit, claiming the industry was liable for state-paid hospital costs arising from smoking-related diseases such as lung cancer. The full case is expected to come to trial during 1997.

A Jacksonville, Fla., court last summer handed the tobacco industry its biggest court loss yet in the long-running legal battle with smoking-disease victims when it awarded $750,000 to a lung cancer sufferer who had smoked for half a century. The defendant was the Brown & Williamson unit of B.A.T Industries Plc.
